title: Claim: heap-root-is-minimum
body: After heapq.heapify, the first element of the plain list is the minimum.

title: Claim: heappop-yields-sorted-order
body: Repeated heappop returns the elements in ascending order.

title: Claim: heapify-is-linear
body: heapify on n items costs about n, not n log n: doubling n roughly doubles the time, not more.

title: Claim: nlargest-beats-a-full-sort-for-small-k
body: heapq.nlargest(k, data) for small k is faster than sorting all of data and slicing.

title: Complexity: heap[0] (peek minimum)
body:
**O(1)**

the minimum is always at index 0

title: Complexity: heapq.heappush
body:
**O(log n)**

sift up at most log n levels

title: Complexity: heapq.heappop
body:
**O(log n)**

move the last item to the root, sift down

title: Complexity: heapq.nlargest(k, data)
body:
**O(n log k)**

keeps a heap of size k while scanning

title: Q1: Why does heapq store a heap in a plain list?
body:
A. Lists are the only mutable sequence in Python
B. The children of index i are at 2i+1 and 2i+2, so no node objects are needed
C. heapq only works on tuples
D. A heap is faster to store as a list because it stays sorted

**B.** The array layout gives the tree's parent and child positions by arithmetic, with no pointers to manage.

title: Q2: What is the cost of heapq.heappop on a heap of n items?
body:
A. O(1)
B. O(log n)
C. O(n)
D. O(n log n)

**B.** The last item moves to the root and sifts down at most one path, about log n levels.

title: Q3: heapq is a min-heap. How do you get the largest value first?
body:
A. Call heapq.heappop(max=True)
B. Push the negated values and pop the smallest
C. Sort the list first
D. Use a deque instead

**B.** The most negative number is the one with the largest magnitude, so negating turns max into min.

title: Q4: Why is building a heap from a list with heapify faster than
body:
A. heapify skips the comparisons
B. heapify is O(n) bottom-up, while n pushes cost O(n log n) in total
C. heappush cannot be used on lists
D. heapify sorts the list first

**B.** Sifting down from the middle does less total work than sifting up each item as it arrives.

title: LeetCode 347: Top K Frequent Elements
body:
**Pattern**: top-k selection

**Why**: Only the k most frequent matter, so a heap of size k beats sorting every distinct value.

**Python**: `collections.Counter, then heapq.nlargest`

title: LeetCode 215: Kth Largest Element in an Array
body:
**Pattern**: top-k selection

**Why**: A min-heap of the k largest seen so far keeps its root as the answer.

**Python**: `heapq: heappush, and heappop when the heap grows past k`

title: LeetCode 23: Merge k Sorted Lists
body:
**Pattern**: k-way merge

**Why**: One head per list in the heap gives the next smallest value across all lists in O(log k).

**Python**: `heapq.heappush / heappop, or heapq.merge`
